situation: A senior asks what you thought of her presentation.
say: It was very nice, ma'am. Perfect.
better: The data was strong. I'd cut a few slides in the middle so the main point comes sooner.
also: Clear and well researched. The ending could be punchier.
weak: Too long and boring, honestly.
Superb, ma'am, no changes needed at all.
why: Useful opinions are specific; 'very nice' tells her nothing.

situation: You have an idea in a team meeting but feel too junior to share it.
say: This may be a stupid question, but maybe we could possibly...
better: I have a suggestion. What if we asked users before building this?
also: One idea: let's test this with ten users first.
weak: Sorry, sorry, small point, ignore if it's wrong...
I don't know if this makes sense, but...
why: Don't shrink your idea before people even hear it.

situation: At dinner, someone asks what you thought of a film everyone loved.
say: Worst film ever made. Total waste of money.
better: Honestly, it didn't work for me. The second half dragged. But I can see why people loved it.
also: Not my kind of film, but the music was great.
weak: Only fools liked that film.
Ya, it was nice, nice.
why: An honest view, a reason, and room for other tastes.

situation: In class, the teacher asks what you think a poem means.
say: Ma'am, it is a very nice poem with a good message.
better: I think the poem is really about loneliness. The empty house in the last lines shows it.
also: To me it feels more angry than sad, because the lines are short and sharp.
weak: Ma'am, whatever the guidebook says.
It is very beautiful and meaningful, ma'am.
why: A specific claim with evidence from the text beats general praise.

situation: You're giving your view in a placement group discussion.
say: In my personal opinion, I think that according to me...
better: I think the company should hire locally first. Here's why.
also: My view is simple: hire locally first, then expand.
weak: According to me, as per my view, I feel...
I would like to humbly put forth my opinion that...
why: Say 'I think' once, then get to the point.

situation: Everyone in the meeting supports an idea, but you have doubts.
say: Ya, ya, sounds good.
better: I may be the odd one out, but I'm worried about the cost. Can we look at that first?
also: Before we decide, can I raise one concern?
weak: This idea will fail, mark my words.
Ok, majority wins, I'll keep quiet.
why: Voice doubt early and politely; silence is not agreement.

situation: A relative asks if working from home is 'real work'.
say: Aunty, you won't understand. Times have changed.
better: I think it is, if the work gets done. My office tracks results, not hours at a desk.
also: For me it works well, though I do miss people sometimes.
weak: Aunty, please, it's not the 1990s.
Ya aunty, you're right, it's not real work.
why: Explain your view with an example instead of dismissing them.

situation: In class, you're asked whether exams should be replaced by projects.
say: Exams are useless. Projects are the best.
better: Projects test real skills, so I lean towards them. But exams are harder to cheat in, so maybe a mix.
also: I'd keep both: projects for skills, a short exam for the basics.
weak: Both are good and both are bad, so it depends.
Exams are best because that's how it's always been.
why: Take a side, but show you weighed the other one.

situation: A friend asks what you honestly think of his startup idea.
say: No offence, but this idea is useless.
better: I like that it solves a real problem. I'm less sure people will pay for it. Have you asked them?
also: The idea is strong; the pricing is what I'd test first.
weak: It's amazing, bro, you'll be the next unicorn!
Startups fail anyway, just take a job.
why: Honest feedback lands better when it starts with something true and good.

situation: New data makes you change the view you gave in last week's meeting.
say: Actually, I was always a bit doubtful only.
better: Last week I backed option A. With these numbers, I now think B is better.
also: I've changed my mind, and here's what changed it.
weak: I never really supported A, you misunderstood.
Whatever the team decides, I'm fine.
why: Changing your view openly, with a reason, shows good judgement.

situation: An interviewer asks, 'What do you think about AI taking jobs?'
say: Sir, it is a double-edged sword. It has pros and cons.
better: I think it will change most jobs more than it removes them. People who learn to use it will gain.
also: Some jobs will go and new ones will come. The gap in between is the real problem.
weak: Sir, AI is the future, so it is good.
Sir, it depends on many factors.
why: Skip the cliché; give a clear claim you can defend.

situation: You strongly believe in a decision, but your team is wavering.
say: Trust me, I know. Just do it my way.
better: I'm confident about this. We tried the other route last year and lost two clients. I'd stick with this.
also: I feel strongly here, and I'll own it if it goes wrong.
weak: If you don't agree, I'm not responsible.
Fine, do whatever, I don't care.
why: Conviction needs a reason and ownership, not just force.

situation: At dinner, someone asks if you'd move abroad for a better job.
say: Obviously, bro. There's nothing for us here.
better: I'd consider it for a few years, mainly for the experience. Long term, I'd like to come back.
also: Maybe. It depends on the role more than the country.
weak: Abroad is far better in every single way.
Never. People who leave are selfish.
why: A clear answer with your reasons, without judging other people's choices.

situation: Your father wants you to do an MBA, but you think differently.
say: Papa, it's my life. Let me decide.
better: I see why you think an MBA would help. I'd rather work for two years first and then decide.
also: Can I tell you why I'm leaning another way?
weak: Papa, MBA is useless nowadays.
Ok papa, whatever you say.
why: Acknowledge their view, then state yours clearly and kindly.

situation: In class, you agree with a classmate and want to add something.
say: Ma'am, same as what he said.
better: I agree with Riya, and I'd add one thing: nobody has counted the cost of the scheme.
also: Building on Riya's point, there's also the question of who pays.
weak: Ma'am, my point is also the same only.
Riya already said it, so nothing from my side.
why: Agree, then add something new so your voice counts.

situation: Your manager wants a quick view on which of two vendors to choose.
say: Both are good only, sir. Whatever you decide.
better: I'd go with the second vendor. They cost a bit more, but they deliver on time.
also: Quick answer: vendor two, mainly for reliability.
weak: Let me think and get back to you in a few days.
Both have their pros and cons, sir.
why: A quick, clear pick with one reason saves everyone's time.

situation: A friend says all influencers are fake and asks if you agree.
say: Ya, totally. All of them are frauds.
better: Some are, for sure. But a few teach really useful things. I'd judge them one by one.
also: Many are, but 'all' is too strong for me.
weak: You're just jealous of them.
Whatever, I don't even watch reels.
why: Avoid sweeping words like 'all'; they make a view easy to knock down.

situation: You want to give your honest view on a colleague's proposal.
say: Frankly speaking, honestly, to tell you the truth, it's not good.
better: I don't think it will work as it is. The budget is too tight. Could we cut the scope?
also: My honest view: good idea, wrong timing.
weak: I'm a very straightforward person, so I'll say it's bad.
Not bad, not bad, it's ok types.
why: Just say the honest thing; you don't need to announce your honesty.

situation: Your professor says social media only harms students, and you see it differently.
say: Sir, that's not true at all.
better: I partly agree, sir. But I've learnt a lot from online lectures. Could the harm depend on how it's used?
also: Could I share a different experience, sir?
weak: Sir, you're from another generation, so...
Sir, you're right, it's very bad.
why: Disagree with a teacher by sharing evidence, not by dismissing them.

situation: At a chai stall, someone asks your take on the latest team selection.
say: Selectors are mad. Total politics.
better: I'd have picked the younger bowler. His recent form is better, and we need pace in Australia.
also: Tough call, but I'd back form over reputation.
weak: Whatever, cricket is all fixed anyway.
I don't know, they know better.
why: A view with one fact sounds smarter than an angry label.

situation: In a meeting about a contract, someone asks you, a non-lawyer, what you think.
say: I'm not a lawyer, so I can't say anything.
better: I'm not a legal expert, but as a user, this clause looks confusing. Worth checking with legal.
also: Outside my area, but one thing stood out to me.
weak: It looks fine, just sign it.
No idea, ask someone else.
why: Mark your limit, then still offer what you can see.

situation: Friends ask which phone they should buy.
say: This phone is the best, full stop. Everything else is rubbish.
better: For me this one is best, because the camera and battery suit how I use it. What's your budget?
also: I love mine, but what do you mostly use your phone for?
weak: Just buy it, don't argue with me.
All phones are the same, buy anything.
why: Mark an opinion as yours, and fit it to their needs.

situation: Your project group must choose a topic, and you strongly prefer one.
say: Guys, let's do my topic. It's the best. Final.
better: I'd vote for water shortage. We can collect local data ourselves, which makes the project stronger.
also: Can I make the case for my topic in one minute?
weak: If we don't do my topic, I'm not working.
Anything is fine, guys, you decide.
why: Persuade with a reason that helps the group, not with pressure.

situation: A friend asks if a new diet will help her lose weight.
say: Hundred percent it will work. My cousin lost ten kilos.
better: It might help, but I'm not sure. A doctor or dietitian would know better than me.
also: It worked for my cousin, but bodies differ. Maybe check with a doctor.
weak: Diets are a scam, don't waste your time.
Guaranteed results, just start tomorrow.
why: Match your confidence to what you actually know.

situation: In a group discussion, you get thirty seconds to sum up your view.
say: So, so, that's all, I think, ya. Thank you.
better: To sum up: start small, measure the results, and expand only what works. Thank you.
also: My bottom line: test first, scale later.
weak: So, in conclusion, there are many points and all are important.
That's it, nothing more from my side, I guess.
why: End with one clear line people will remember.
